title: Tall Trees
summary: Famous forest giants, distinctive tree species and four familiar height references become sorting, comparison and number challenges.
dataNote: Heights are sourced comparison values: named-tree measurements, exceptional species examples or stated mature ranges. Each card explains its basis; photos of species are not height measurements. Living trees change. Dave is 6 ft and Geoffrey is 18 ft; stacks are rounded estimates. The four stats all describe height, so this pack does not recommend Top Trumps.

audience.readingLevel: short tree facts with rounded height math

cards.name: Dave the Human
cards.imageAlt: Standing human height reference beside a ruler
cards.imageCredit: Burrow original SVG
cards.fact: Dave is our imaginary 6-foot person. His fixed height makes it easy to picture how tall a tree is.

metadata.accuracyNote: Fictional 6-foot teaching reference, not an average human height. All Dave stacks divide the displayed height in feet by 6 and round to the nearest whole Dave.

sources.label: Burrow teaching reference
sources.note: Dave is a deliberately defined 6-foot reference; meter and stack values are derived.

readingPrompts: How many Daves tall is a 60-foot tree?

cards.name: Geoffrey the Giraffe
cards.imageAlt: Tall giraffe standing in a park
cards.imageCredit: Muhammad Mahdi Karim / Wikimedia Commons / GFDL 1.2 (https://www.gnu.org/licenses/old-licenses/fdl-1.2.html); local resized copy
cards.fact: A giraffe can stand about 18 feet tall. We use that height for Geoffrey, our giraffe-sized tree ruler.

metadata.accuracyNote: Geoffrey is a fictional 18-foot teaching reference, within adult giraffe heights; individual giraffes vary. Giraffe stacks divide feet by 18 and round to the nearest whole giraffe, except the human reference.

sources.label: Smithsonian: Giraffe
sources.note: Adult height reference of 5.5 m / 18 ft.

readingPrompts: What tree cards are more than ten giraffes tall?

cards.name: English Oak

cards.fact: English oaks grow from acorns. Their broad branches and leaves provide food and shelter for many woodland animals.

metadata.accuracyNote: The 35 m height is a comparison example within the usual 20–40 m mature range, not a record or a measurement of this leafy branch. Native across much of Europe and into western Asia.

sources.label: Woodland Trust: English oak

cards.fact: Atlantis launched standing upright beside its fuel tank and two boosters. Together, this shuttle stack was about 184 feet tall.

metadata.accuracyNote: Height is for the full upright launch stack, not the orbiter alone or its height on the runway. It is a size reference, not a tree.

sources.label: NASA: The Space Shuttle

metadata.accuracyNote: Species card with a 67 m comparison example, near the 66 m-plus planted trees described by Forest Research. The photo shows a Douglas fir in Germany, not the named Welsh record tree. Location describes the native range.

sources.label: Forest Research: Douglas fir

metadata.accuracyNote: The 73 m height is an illustrative tall karri within the species range. It is not a measurement of the pictured trees, and this card makes no European record claim. Karri is a eucalyptus, not merely a relative.

cards.name: General Sherman
cards.imageAlt: The General Sherman giant sequoia tree
cards.imageCredit: Tuxyso / Wikimedia Commons / CC BY-SA 3.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/); local resized copy
cards.fact: General Sherman has the largest trunk volume of any known living tree. A taller tree can still have a much thinner trunk.

metadata.accuracyNote: Named individual; NPS height is 274.9 ft / 83.8 m, rounded to 275 ft. Largest refers to trunk volume, not height.

sources.label: National Park Service: General Sherman
sources.note: Height 274.9 ft / 83.8 m and largest living tree by trunk volume.

cards.name: Big Ben
cards.imageAlt: Elizabeth Tower, often called Big Ben, in London
cards.imageCredit: Dave Bezaire / Wikimedia Commons / CC BY-SA 2.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/2.0/); local resized copy
cards.fact: Big Ben is the bell inside Elizabeth Tower in London. The tower rises about 316 feet, high enough to compare with forest giants.

metadata.accuracyNote: 316 ft is the height of Elizabeth Tower, not the bell named Big Ben. Meter value is rounded from the feet comparison.

sources.label: UK Parliament: The towers of Parliament
sources.note: Elizabeth Tower is 96.3 m / 316 ft; Big Ben is its main bell.

cards.name: Centurion
cards.imageAlt: Centurion, a very tall Eucalyptus regnans tree in Tasmania
cards.imageCredit: Eucalyptus 99 / Wikimedia Commons / CC BY-SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/); local resized copy
cards.fact: Centurion is a mountain ash in Tasmania. Fire damaged this giant, showing how even the tallest living trees can lose height.

metadata.accuracyNote: Named individual. Mifsud et al. (2025), Table 3, lists 96.5 m with living leaves at its top; rounded prose in that paper says 96 m. The earlier 100.5 m figure is historical. Trees can grow or lose height.

sources.label: Mifsud and colleagues: giant eucalypts, 2025
sources.note: Field measurements, Table 3 and discussion; includes post-fire tree condition. Read with the 2025 corrigendum.

cards.name: Coast Redwood
cards.imageAlt: Coast redwoods towering beside a road in a California forest
cards.imageCredit: Acroterion / Wikimedia Commons / CC BY-SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/); resized
cards.fact: Coast redwoods grow in the foggy forests of coastal California and Oregon. A tree named Hyperion reached more than 116 meters.

location.label: Native to coastal California and southwestern Oregon, United States

metadata.accuracyNote: Species card using Hyperion’s 2019 tape-drop measurement of 116.07 m, rounded to 381 ft / 116 m. This is an exceptional individual, not a typical height. The photograph shows coast redwoods, not a claimed image of Hyperion.

sources.label: Guinness World Records: tallest living tree
sources.note: Hyperion measured 116.07 m in 2019.

sources.label: National Park Service: Hyperion
sources.note: Species, protected location and tallest-tree context.

sources.note: Native range from southern Oregon to central California and the role of coastal fog.

cards.name: South Tibetan Cypress
cards.imageAlt: South Tibetan cypress growing in a steep valley
cards.imageCredit: Zhangzhugang; crop and color balance by MPF / Wikimedia Commons / GFDL 1.2 or later (https://www.gnu.org/licenses/old-licenses/fdl-1.2.html); local resized copy
cards.fact: A South Tibetan cypress measured at 102.3 meters made this species one of the tallest known trees in Asia.

metadata.accuracyNote: Species card. The 102.3 m number is an exceptional individual measured in the Yarlung Zangbo Grand Canyon in 2023, not a typical species height or the pictured trees. Scientific name used by the measurement paper: Cupressus austrotibetica.

sources.label: Peking University: Discovering and measuring giant trees

cards.name: Yellow Meranti
cards.imageAlt: Tall yellow meranti tree in a tropical forest
cards.imageCredit: Annette Teng / Wikimedia Commons
cards.fact: Yellow meranti can rise above the rainforest canopy. Researchers climbed a giant named Menara and lowered a tape to measure its height.

metadata.accuracyNote: Species card; 97.6 m is Menara’s mean-bole-base height: (98.90 + 96.26) / 2 = 97.58 m, rounded. The often quoted 100.8 m starts at the lowest buttress. The older photo illustrates yellow meranti, not Menara. Location describes the measured reference in Sabah, not the whole species range.

sources.label: Shenkin and colleagues: The World’s Tallest Tropical Tree
sources.note: 2019 paper reports 98.90 m and 96.26 m from opposite bole-base points, and 100.8 m from the lowest buttress.
